explanations.explanation: Wrath is it, baker. John says the angels hold the seven final plagues, “…with which the wrath of God is completed.” (Revelation 15:1) Final means final. This is the last set, and the passage says so up front.

I get why harvest popped up. John just watched the earth get harvested with a sickle (Revelation 14:14-16), so the word is still hanging around. But Revelation 15:1 says the plagues are the ones with which “the wrath of God is completed.” That's the word that goes in the blank.

The temple does show up in this passage, friend, and it gets very busy. But the blank isn't about a place. Revelation 15:1 says these final plagues are the ones with which “the wrath of God is completed.” The word is wrath.

True! John says they were “holding harps from God.” (Revelation 15:2) These are the ones who conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, and now they're standing beside the sea of glass. Harps in hand, ready to sing.

This one's true, friend. John says the people beside the sea of glass “were holding harps from God.” (Revelation 15:2) They had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name. And right after the harps comes the singing.

Moses it is. Moses was Israel's leader, and the singers sing “the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb.” (Revelation 15:3) Moses and Israel once sang a song to the LORD beside a sea too (Exodus 15:1). Two names on one song, and John gives us both.

David, Israel's king, is a fair guess with all those harps around. But John never names him here. The song is called “the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb.” (Revelation 15:3) The other name is Moses.

Elijah, the prophet who stood up to Israel's kings, is a big name, friend. But he isn't in this verse. John says they sang “the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb.” (Revelation 15:3) The other name is Moses.
That's the reason they give. They sing, “Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy.” (Revelation 15:4) Notice the word alone. They aren't comparing Him to anybody.

explanations.answer: Because the sea obeys His voice
explanations.explanation: The singers are standing by a sea, so I see how that one sneaks in. But the song never says the sea obeys Him. Their reason is, “For You alone are holy.” (Revelation 15:4)

Plenty of angels in this passage, baker, but nobody sings about their sleep schedule. The song asks, “Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name?” and then gives the reason: “For You alone are holy.” (Revelation 15:4)

The song says the opposite. It says, “All nations will come and worship before You, for Your righteous acts have been revealed.” (Revelation 15:4) All nations, friend, not a few. Easy to miss when you're reading fast.
False is right. The song says, “All nations will come and worship before You, for Your righteous acts have been revealed.” (Revelation 15:4) Not a few nations. All of them.

Bowls, baker. One of the four living creatures gave the angels “seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever.” (Revelation 15:7) A bowl is something you pour out from, and that's what comes next.

Trumpets do play a big part elsewhere in Revelation, so I understand the guess. But in this passage the creature hands over “seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God.” (Revelation 15:7) Bowls are what get poured out in chapter 16.

Crowns are a good guess, since Revelation has crowns in other places. Here, though, the living creature gives the angels “seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God.” (Revelation 15:7) Bowls, not crowns.

The door gets shut on this one. John says, “…no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.” (Revelation 15:8) The temple fills with smoke from God's glory and power, and nobody goes in until the plagues are done.

False is right. The temple is filled with smoke from God's glory and His power, and “…no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.” (Revelation 15:8) Nobody walks in until the plagues are done.

explanations.answer: Those with the mark of the beast
explanations.explanation: Right. The sores break out “on those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.” (Revelation 16:2) The text names exactly who gets them. The passage keeps being that specific, so keep reading carefully.

The bowl is poured on the earth, so that's an understandable guess. But the text is more specific. The sores break out “on those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.” (Revelation 16:2)

explanations.answer: Those beside the sea of glass
explanations.explanation: Those folks are standing by the sea of glass holding harps and singing (Revelation 15:2-3), so they're in a very different spot. They're the ones who conquered the beast and its image. The sores go to “those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.” (Revelation 16:2)

Dies. The sea turns to blood “like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died.” (Revelation 16:3) This is a heavy one, friend, and I won't joke about it. The text says every living thing.

Fleeing would mean they got away, baker, and the text doesn't say that. It says the sea turned to blood “like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died.” (Revelation 16:3) It's a heavy verse.

Hiding would mean they had somewhere to go. Revelation 16:3 says the sea turned to blood “like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died.” This part is heavy, so we'll just read it plainly.

explanations.answer: They spilled the blood of saints and prophets
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the angel gives. He says, “For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets, and You have given them blood to drink, as they deserve.” (Revelation 16:6) I think this one hurts to read. But the angel of the waters states the reason right there.

explanations.answer: They poisoned the rivers and springs
explanations.explanation: The rivers and springs turned to blood, so I see where that comes from. But the angel never says the people poisoned them. His reason is, “For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets…” (Revelation 16:6)

explanations.answer: They tore down the temple of God
explanations.explanation: The temple is all over this passage, friend, so it's a natural guess. But the angel of the waters doesn't mention it as his reason. He says, “For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets…” (Revelation 16:6)

True! John hears the altar reply, “Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments.” (Revelation 16:7) The angel of the waters speaks, then the altar agrees. Two voices, same words about God's judgments.
This one's true, baker. John says, “And I heard the altar reply: ‘Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments.’” (Revelation 16:7) The altar agrees with the angel of the waters.

Not this time, friend. The people were scorched by intense heat, “and they cursed the name of God, who had authority over these plagues.” (Revelation 16:9) The text adds, “Yet they did not repent and give Him glory.”
False is right. John says they “cursed the name of God, who had authority over these plagues. Yet they did not repent and give Him glory.” (Revelation 16:9) The heat came, and repenting did not.

explanations.answer: They curse the God of heaven
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The men “curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores. Yet they did not repent of their deeds.” (Revelation 16:11) It's a hard verse to read, and I think it's meant to be.
I wish the text went that way, baker, but it doesn't. Instead the men “curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores.” (Revelation 16:11) The verse adds, “Yet they did not repent of their deeds.”

It's the beast's throne that gets the darkness, so I see why that came to mind. But the text never says they turn on the beast. It says they “curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores.” (Revelation 16:11)

explanations.answer: To prepare the way for the kings of the East
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the reason given. The sixth angel's bowl goes on the Euphrates, “and its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East.” (Revelation 16:12) The text gives the purpose in the same sentence.

explanations.answer: To let God's people cross over safely
explanations.explanation: A river drying up so people can cross sounds like a story you might have heard before. But this verse doesn't say that. It says the water “was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East.” (Revelation 16:12)

explanations.answer: To end the plague of blood in the rivers
explanations.explanation: The rivers did turn to blood back in verse 4, so I get the link. But the text doesn't connect the two. The Euphrates dries up “to prepare the way for the kings of the East.” (Revelation 16:12)
Battle, baker. The spirits go out to the kings of the earth “to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.” (Revelation 16:14) The text says what the kings are being gathered for.
Worship is a good word, and it shows up in this passage in other places. But here the spirits go out “to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.” (Revelation 16:14)
A big crowd of kings could be for a lot of things, friend. But Revelation 16:14 says the spirits go out “to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.” Battle is the word.

True. Right after “Behold, I am coming like a thief,” the verse says, “Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed, so that he will not go naked and let his shame be exposed.” (Revelation 16:15) A blessing in the middle of all those bowls.

This one's true, baker. After “Behold, I am coming like a thief,” comes, “Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed…” (Revelation 16:15) It's one verse, and the blessing comes right behind the warning.
“It is done!” That's the loud voice from the throne in the temple. (Revelation 16:17) The seventh bowl is the last of the seven, and those are the words that come with it.
No second round here, friend. The seventh angel is the last of the seven, and the voice from the throne says, “It is done!” (Revelation 16:17)
The temple was opened back in Revelation 15:5, so it's still on your mind. But after the seventh bowl, the voice from the throne says, “It is done!” (Revelation 16:17)

explanations.answer: Greatest since people came on the earth
explanations.explanation: That's what John says. It's “a great earthquake the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth—so mighty was the great quake.” (Revelation 16:18) It was preceded by lightning, rumblings and thunder. In all the earth's history, nothing like it.

explanations.answer: Strong enough to shake only the great city
explanations.explanation: The great city does get hit hard, and it splits into three parts. But the text says the quake is “the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth.” (Revelation 16:18) That's far bigger than one city.

explanations.answer: Mighty but over in a single moment
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give us a time on this quake, baker, so a single moment is an addition. What it does say is that it was “a great earthquake the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth.” (Revelation 16:18) That's the part to hold on to.
Collapse. The great city was split into three parts, “and the cities of the nations collapsed.” (Revelation 16:19) The quake doesn't stop at one city.
Nobody's celebrating in this verse, friend. The text says the great city was split into three parts, “and the cities of the nations collapsed.” (Revelation 16:19)
Rebuilding would come later, and this verse doesn't go there. It says the great city was split into three parts, “and the cities of the nations collapsed.” (Revelation 16:19)

True. The verse says, “And God remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath.” (Revelation 16:19) The cup is given to Babylon the great, and the verse names it plainly.
This one's true, baker. Revelation 16:19 says God “remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath.” Babylon the great is the one who gets the cup.

True. After the hail, the verse says, “And men cursed God for the plague of hail, because it was so horrendous.” (Revelation 16:21) Hailstones of almost a hundred pounds each, and the response is the same as before. It's a heavy way to end the bowls.

This one's true, friend. The text says, “And men cursed God for the plague of hail, because it was so horrendous.” (Revelation 16:21) The hailstones weighed almost a hundred pounds each, and cursing is what the men did.
